Messages.Author: islando...@aol.com
Messages.Body:
This is a serious post and I want to start a serious discussion, so
please don't flame me with "OMGZ if you can't see weenies are broken
then you're dumb". This is my experience with weenies and I'm not
looking to ignore it, but rather to understand whatever all of you see
when you tell me weenies are broken.

---------------

I started playing Tremere, but when Sabbat came out, I immediately
began trying to build a Pander deck. Before I even saw Legacy of
Pander, my idea was to combine their Potence (Jimmy Dunn, Mitchell,
Rex, and the Ghouled Street Thug) with some skill cards and some
Embraces (which could, at the time, get skill cards.) Nobody really
used either weenie voters OR potence very much/very well in my
playgroup, so the deck was sort of an amalgam of everything I thought
was broken that nobody was breaking.

Vote pushing was allowed, and of course intercept was quite rare back
in those days. Naturally the deck was able to steamroll over people
pretty effectively. (How I long for those days!) Well, in time, I
discovered the Seattle playgroup, and brought my Panders with me. By
now vote pushing had been removed from the rules, but the deck was
still interesting and quite powerful. Weenie Potence with Con Boons
for 8+, if you will. I started working a job about 90 miles in the
other direction from the Seattle playgroup, and I wasn't able to
attend for 6 months or so, when the qualifier made it a priority.

That six months was the biggest metagame shift I'd ever seen.
Suddenly, all the stealth-bleed was replaced by toolboxes and
intercept-combat. There were a few voters, but more or less, the huge
payoff of the Con Boon with the minimal risk of being blocked had
turned into the surefire way to get someone to block me. Having
recently taken out the Potence, since fights seemed increasingly rare,
I was the least prepared for this I ever was. I had one Gangrel block
me 11 times in 3 turns. Not one Gangrel player, ONE GANGREL. He was
my predator in round two and then my prey in round 3 (yuck).

I tried to get them to work, and to a degree I had--but the deck was
no longer a true weenie deck. My understanding of the weenie deck is
mostly that it uses its huge number of actions to overwhelm an
opponent--and I don't really use the weenies for actions at all. I
bring out Marie Faucigny, who calls Con Boons and plays Private
Audience so that they pass. That's all the Panders are--more pool,
until I have enough to pass Legacy of Pander in the same way and THEN
I can try to lunge.

Yeah it's slow. Real slow. And it gets most of the table hate that
weenies get. But you know what? It isn't an auto-loss to weenie AUS,
the way every other version of that deck is. Marie can do a vote at 6
or 7 stealth without breaking a sweat. In fact, the less the deck was
taking actions with the newly-fragile Panders, the better it was
doing. I considered putting in Nightmares Upon Nightmares, to
convince the table that I wasn't going to act with the vampires and
maybe even get some free discards in the process, but decided against
it cause I often have to use them to lunge with.

Don't think I'm crazy. Various incarnations of the "no Panders act"
Panders won two qualifiers and got 5th at the 2005 EC.

My point? That in my experience personally, both in the local
metagame and in large tournaments, the trend is that a bunch of
vampires with 1 or 2 stealth all trying to act are going to end up
next to a single Sport Bike, or Carna, or Bowl, or all three, or
Howler...

You get my point. Only by stopping the Panders from doing anything
but giving me pool could I get the deck to work. And I have seen
weenie breed decks, and they're usually foiled by Domain Challenge,
Ancilla Empowerment, Anarchist Uprising, or just sitting next to
someone with a handful of Auspex. If they aren't, BTW, I see them
play Palla Grande or Week of Nightmares and sweep the table--but
that's if.

So in conclusion, I've seen weenies at their best. Times when vote-
pushing and a dearth of intercept meant I could go through a table
like hot fangs through butter. But I've seen good vampires with
incidental titles increase, casual intercept increase, dedicated
intercept sharply increase, and of course political decks remain a
force, bringing with them the weenie-hosing votes. I think the time
that a bunch of 1-caps could just rely on going unblocked is behind
us, and weenies need to think about their delivery system and payload
in order to get anything done. CEL on a 4 cap? Maybe. POT on a 4
cap? Sure. DOM on a 4 cap? Quite likely. Nothing on a bunch of 1
caps? Not at all.

Years of coming closer and closer to this conclusion, and then at the
EC last year, a strict weenie deck, all 1- and 2-caps, comes out guns
blazing--literally--and blows three tables away with concealed weapon,
cheap guns, Dragon's Breath Rounds, and sometimes Graverobbing.

Now, I respect the player who did it--both for designing it
effectively and for being one hell of a player. But I still ask: Has
this crap been going on all along, and I just haven't seen any of it
in the last 7 years of casual and 5 years of championship-level play?
(Discount Anarch Revolt weenies, as that couldn't happen today.) I
don't see how everyone can tell me weenies are totally broken unless
they either don't mean the 1- and 2-caps that I mean (rather the 4-
caps with superior disciplines in common), or unless their experience
diverges REALLY significantly from mine.

Thank you for reading my story, and I hope someone can tell me what it
is about weenies--not conceptually, I understand they have a lot of
actions--what it is that makes them so feared.

-- Brian

Messages.Author: mummy
Messages.Body:
> Thank you for reading my story, and I hope someone can tell me what it
> is about weenies--not conceptually, I understand they have a lot of
> actions--what it is that makes them so feared.

Hi Brian,

so it took be a bit of rereading to figure out that by "Empirical
Evidence of Weenies' Brokenness", you meant "GIVE ME Empirical
Evidence of Weenies' Brokenness", rather than "This post will provide
all of you with Empirical Evidence of Weenies' Brokenness".

I don't think they're broken. I think, in a game where number of
actions is pivotal, weenies are very efficient, giving you a lot of
bang for your buck. If your deck concept is something other than just
weenie swarm, and your deck concept fails, you can still fall back on
weenie swarm. Often, that is good enough. I have had that experience
most notably with my Cryptic Mission deck. It is hindered by a single
Hunting Ground, and foiled by even a small degree of permanent
intercap. Even in those cases, however, I still have 6+ minions with
which to bleed, and that often wins the game. Legacy of Pander and
Ghouled Street Thug decks probably work in a similar way, though I
don't have much experience with them.

You are correct that weenies are less powerful than they used to be,
and you mentioned a couple key factors (anti-weenie votes, prohibition
of vote-pushing). Also, Majesty and Catatonic Fear now cost a blood,
which hinders significantly the presence weenie deck. The pure 1- and
2-cap weenie bleed deck is also hindered by additional untap cards (On
the Que Vive, Special Report). No question that Friendmaker decks are
no longer taking the world by storm.

Overall, I suspect that the general consensus is that weenies are a
strong element of any strategy, and a weenie bleed deck is sure to win
a frequent VP and also the occasional game, but the case for weenies
being broken is a lot harder to make.

cheers,
Jon

Messages.Author: Robert Goudie
Messages.Body:
On Feb 27, 11:48 am, "mummy" <mummydirtys...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> Overall, I suspect that the general consensus is that weenies are a
> strong element of any strategy, and a weenie bleed deck is sure to win
> a frequent VP and also the occasional game, but the case for weenies
> being broken is a lot harder to make.

I think the weenie problem is an actual flaw in the game design. The
theoretical brokeness (yes, I know Brian isn't looking for theory) is
seen in the case that four influence can be spent on four 1-caps that
can bleed for four or block 4 zero stealth bleeds versus the case that
four influence can be spent on one 4-cap that can bleed for one or
block 1 bleed (aka "The Sheldon Situation").

This flaw in the V:TES design has never been fixed directly. LSJ has
done an admirable job of patching this flaw by creating cards that
punish weenies as well as by continuing to provide boosts to the
fatties. I'm very comfortable with the current level of things where
weenies are still playable but not, imo, too powerful.

-Robert

> punish weenies as well as by continuing to provide boosts to the
> fatties. I'm very comfortable with the current level of things where

I think recent card releases has patched this flaw from the other
direction as well. Not just limiting weenies, but also helping out
ol' Sheldon. Freak Drive has gone from being a rare (Jyhad) to being
a highly sought-after uncommon (Cam Ed) to being an uncommon-that-is-
still-sought-after-but-reasonably-easy-to-get. Not to mention Forced
March for the cel for vampires, Mylan Horseed, Helicopter, what-have-
you. In the last year or two, I very commonly see huge vampire take
and block multiple actions, and that helps close the Sheldon gap as
well.

Which is great, because, considering how many huge vampires there are,
it's nice to see them be playable competitively. I'm a big fan of
card games where you can play the game with the cards.

-Jon

Messages.Author: Jeff Kuta
Messages.Body:


There is only one basic game design rule that is anti-weenie:

TORPOR

It costs 2 blood to Leave Torpor and 2 blood to Rescue. A deck full of
1-caps cannot leave torpor without using cards. Everything else favors
them because they get to take so many actions. Additionally, hunting
is at default +1 stealth, which means some card or ability must grant
+1 intercept to block.

Everyone should just play with Justine, Elder of Dallas, if they're so
concerned about weenies. Get her a Bowl and a Flak Jacket and you're
golden. ;)

Jeff

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <Lm2Fh.1389$LF6...@newssvr11.news.prodigy.net>, LSJ

<vte...@white-wolf.com> writes:
>The above only show it is a flaw if each minion gets to tap only once
>(or if combat isn't the natural result of blocking, or some other
>change to the rules that alters the attrition rate of weenies in
>comparison to non-weenies) and when weenies can play and pay for the
>same combos that larger vampires with more Disciplines can.

I agree up to a point.

In general, I would say that the most direct ousting actions in the game
are bleeding. There may be specific screwball games where it's
completely hosed but, I think, most people would agree that bleeding is
the most direct route to victory, across the myriad permutations of the
game as a whole. Followed up to that, vote is also a direct ousting
mechanism (assuming the player uses them as damage votes), with similar
disclaimers to bleed. Everything else is typically weaker.

Now, my two 4 cap vampires (for example) can take two bleed actions -
and probably two fairly meaty bleed actions. Kindred Spirits, Govern
the Unaligned, Lost in Crowds, Social Charm etc. are all available and
fairly cheap. When my 8 cap untaps, he can't take a second bleed
action, and so we presumably have to hope that the bleed he does plus
the secondary, weaker action equal two bleeds.

But this leads to a problem. Because bleed is so prevalent, bleed
defence is pretty common and, specifically, bleed bounce. Though my 8
cap will - presumably - have some superior disciplines and - presumably
- get a point or two of extra bleed as a result, I am commensurately
more exposed to bleed bounce. Instead of two bleeds for 3, I have one
bleed for 4/5 (and a secondary weaker action, to make up for the gap)
which is more vulnerable to bounce and more vulnerable to Archon
Investigation.

And the "eggs in one basket" syndrome is not just there. Against one 8
cap, I need one lucky break and I can pound him into the dirt. When
compared to the vulnerability of two 4 caps, or two 3s and a 2, or
whatever, it's not just a case of the 8 cap being equal to the offensive
capability but potentially superior, to compensate for this problem.

That this extra power is or isn't available in practise is far harder to
establish, however!

--
James Coupe

Huh. But the four weenies get to tap four times per turn, while the one
4-cap gets to tap once per turn. How does the flaw Robert showed not
persist through the entire game?

I mean yeah, complex system and all, but the flaw is the flaw and it's still
there. It's maybe more persistent when you talk about four 2-caps compared
to one 8-cap, but it exists at all levels of the "pool cost to actions"
ratio between small versus large vampires, and the large vampires need a lot
of patches to really compete on even ground. Disciplines mostly don't do it
since you can get superior disciplines on small vampires without that much
trouble (and in a lot of cases, inferior disciplines are close enough to the
strength of superior that you can get by without superior anyway). Titles
do sometimes, but there are titling votes that weenies can use. The basic
rule-set of the game really has very little love for big vampires at all -
they have to rely on cardtext.

Josh

Boon is still quite good, but that's not what most people mean by
weenie deck. The weenie bleed/blitz vote style deck seems like its on
the way out. They are just too predicable and fragile. They win the
two player game but not a 4-5 player game.

The can still ruin your day. If their predator pops up with weenie
DOM, good players will recognize the threat, hang their head and sigh,
the then try to hang in and back oust- hoping to conserve enough
resources to get to play their game at some point. The weenie deck
might get the 1 vp but will have been ganged up upon, and then face a
prey #2 who has had time and no pressure.

The more players get to know "the drill" the less often they play
those decktypes.

Other types of weenie decks suffer from different sets of problem -
but predictability and minion fragility are common themes. I would say
the metgame is moving towards the fatties. Big guys that don't vote,
block, bounce, or multi-act very well (like say !Brujah and Assamites)
don't get much love. But most everyone else seems to be doing just
fine.

I'm a little surprised to the "weenies are broken" cries coming back.

-Ben Swainbank

I think that the power of weenies comes from their speed, not
necessarily by the quality of the actions they can take. If a Meth
couldn't actually bring out four 1-caps at the end of their first
influence phase, then we might have something useful.

Here are the current rules for the Influence phase:

"During your influence phase you may spend your [four] transfers as
follows:

* Spend one transfer to move 1 blood counter from your pool to a
vampire in your uncontrolled region.
* Spend two transfers to move 1 blood counter from a vampire in
your uncontrolled region to your pool.
* Spend four transfers and burn a pool to move a vampire from your
crypt to your uncontrolled region (drawing from the top, as always).

At the end of your influence phase, any vampire in your uncontrolled
region with a number of blood counters on him equal to (or more than)
his capacity becomes controlled. The vampire is turned face up and
moved to the ready region, untapped. The counters are kept on him to
represent his blood (counters in excess of his capacity drain off
immediately as usual)."

Suppose it were slightly different:

First, you would max out at five transfers instead of four.

During your influence phase you may spend your [five] transfers as
follows:

* Spend one transfer to move 1 blood counter from your pool to a
vampire in your uncontrolled region.
* Spend two transfers to move 1 blood counter from a vampire in
your uncontrolled region to your pool.
* Spend four transfers and burn a pool to move a vampire from your
crypt to your uncontrolled region (drawing from the top, as always).
* Spend one transfer to move a vampire with blood greater than or
equal to its capacity from your uncontrolled region to your ready
region.

That's it! There's no automatic move from uncontrolled to ready as
there is now. You gotta pay for it with transfers (but it doesn't cost
pool).

So someone with a crypt full of 1-caps could at best bring two of them
out on turn 1 (3x influences for blood, 2x influences for move from
uncontrolled to ready). The following turn, they would have 4 vampires
ready to rock and roll, but by then everyone else could have a much
larger vampire in play ready to beat on the brats.

This also has a side effect for those who want to bring out larger
vampires. With 10 transfers in your first two turns, 9-caps could make
an appearance on turn 2. If you went first, after 11 transfers on your
third turn, you could have a 10-cap in play. Larger crypts don't feel
the negative impact of this change nearly as much, and that's good by
me.

Any comments on this are more than welcome.

Jeff

Unfortunately addressing widespread issues with new cards is difficult
as almost all card tpyes have a counter (sudden, DI, etc) and
effecting
a dramatic shift solely through new cards is a very slow process, that
if
successful, only encourages the use of the counter-card.

I think it could be agreed that there have been attempts to slow/
hinder
weenies in recent sets (weenie hosing events, Aranthebes, Carvers) but
IMO their effects have not deterred players from playing weenies and
they have
not been effective in controlling weenies due to the cards not being
in play. (Part of
that may be due to uniqueness/once per game of the cards mentioned
above).

Addressing any widespread issue (we can argue whether weenies are
widespread)
with "magic bullet" cards does not work effectively, unless the magic
bullets are
over powered no-brainers and have other uses. Addressing weenies with
a rules
change has the advantage that it does not require deck slots, and
comes into
effect in every game. Its more an innoculation than cure.

As a result I favour a minor rules tweak to hinder weenies somewhat,
but I'm
not sure what that should be yet. Hinder Weenies, empower fatties, I
dunno.

It seems weenie success is still built around what else is at the
table. If no one
other than one player at the table can stomp/stop the weenies, the
weenies can usually
keep ahead of their losses and push ahead through numbers. Put two
combat
decks at a table with weenies and the combat decks can usually work
together to kill the
weenies - but usually at the expense of at least one of the combat
deck's own game. A fast
bleed predator can often kill a weenie deck but usually not before the
weenie kills
one prey (and the fastest bleed decks are small vampires, nearly
weenies themselves).
Wall decks can still stop them IMO if they get moving fast enough and
have transient
intercept and untap. (Atonement, No secrets from the Magaji, Eternal
Vigilance are not a
great help as that action to go get it usually is an action you cannot
afford when sorely
pressed by weenies).

The solutions to weenies through deckbuilding require a significant
portion of decks to adopt
anti-weenie tactics. It has not happened on a large scale here,
probably because weenies are
seldom played (as most players here play for amusement rather than
strict competition, and avoid
weenie decks) but this leaves us open to exploitation by the
occassional weenie deck that does show
up, specially under multideck tournaments. The very fact that socially
we exclude weenies prevents
us from using the cards that might cure it. Lovely, a catch-22. I have
no evidence that this is the case
elsewhere, but I suspect it is to some degree, specially in smaller
groups.

New cards won't address this, new rules might.

-John P.

1/2/? pool for each Elder Power in play/you control."

Note, that my initial Ancient Domain doesn't burn itself at zero
cards. So it'd sit there in play.

Anyways, just some ideas thrown out there. I like the idea, but
automatically found silver bullets need something significant as a
cost, and one that continues to persist after the benefit is gone (AD
above stays in play, and drops your hand size by 1 even after it's
exhausted).

Just my USD$0.0157280

Morgan Vening

> Is it possible we're overlooking some crucial aspect of the game, or

As Ben mentioned, it hurts Tupdogs, but the general case is that it
hurts 1-caps the most. This is a good thing.

Regarding the concern that it will make Govern/Enchant even more
powerful bloating: I don't think that's really a significant issue.
It's pretty rare that you have problems keeping the blood below
capacity, and the benefit of keeping it on seems very small to me (if
you're bloating, you're taking the pool back.)

Also note that this allows the first player to get out a 10 cap on
turn 3, when before the max was a 9-cap. It's also impossible for the
first player to get out any vamp on the first turn without transfer
enhancers. Again, hurting 1-caps. That's fine by me, though.

I say we implement it (or at least start playtesting it!)

Ira

Messages.Author: Jeff Kuta
Messages.Body:


One thing that it does do is eliminate simultaneity at the end of your
influence phase. Before, all vampires/imbued would enter play at the
same time. With this change, there would be discrete moments when
minions moved from uncontrolled to ready with each transfer. I can't
think of any oddball implications, but it would be another side effect
of any such change.

One thing I did keep in mind is that it is still possible (as Meth
Five) to bring out a turn one 4-cap without any influence enhancers.
And Meth One still has transfers enough to bring out a 5-cap first,
which is where the power curve for vampires really starts to kick in
(i.e. instead of inf1 inf2 inf3, you often get SUP1 SUP2 inf3 for
disciplines).

Jeff

I also see a bonus in that when people, currently, forget to bring out a
vamp that is full, or they transferred to the wrong guy and he's
accidentally full, or something, then it causes all sorts of messy 'how
the fuck to we rewind this?' scenarios that such mistakes usually lead
to (and I hate having to make calls on, when judging tournaments).

With the extra transfer point requirement to bring the vamp to the ready
region, there is no longer that mistake to make, and that means less
messy stuff when people screw up. Which is awesome.
